sections.heading: Asking you to stop my sinful will
sections.text: Lord, do whatever mercy requires to keep me from using my life against you. My hands were made to reach for you in faith, but I have used my will to resist you and wound what you love. If something in me has to be restrained, humbled, or taken away so that I do not keep fighting you, then do it. I would rather lose what feeds my sin than keep what keeps me from you.
theological_themes: God’s severe mercy in opposing sin
repentance as turning from a rebellious will
faith as clinging to God rather than striking against him

scripture_references.connection: Jesus uses the strong image of cutting off what leads into sin to show that sin must be dealt with radically, not politely managed. This supports the prayer’s willingness for God to remove or restrain whatever fuels rebellion.

This passage warns that an unbelieving heart can turn away from the living God and be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness. It gives biblical weight to asking God to confront the will before it drifts farther from him.

sections.heading: Seeing the pride under my good actions
sections.text: I am still too attached to being admired. I want honor, respect, intelligence, and a good name more than I want to admit. Even when I do good things, I can feel a hidden part of me checking whether people notice. Father, do not let me be satisfied with merely saying, “I have sinned.” Help me actually see my sin as it is—its ugliness, its motives, and the way it steals worship from you.
theological_themes: the danger of seeking human approval
sin as deeper than outward actions

scripture_references.connection: David asks God to search him and expose any grievous way in him, which fits the prayer’s request not only to name sin but to see it truthfully before God.
Paul contrasts serving Christ with living for human approval. This directly addresses the prayer’s concern that even religious or moral actions can be corrupted by a hunger for reputation.

sections.heading: Confessing the sin that still lives in me
sections.text: Show me the reality of the sin that still clings to me. I know that, in Christ, my old self has been crucified and my sins are forgiven. But I also know they are not yet fully dead in my daily life. Hatred, resentment, ill will, envy, and the craving for praise still rise up in my heart. These sins have been judged at the cross, yet they still try to rule me. This is my lifelong grief and my daily shame: sin does not only come at me from outside; it still finds a place inside me. Lord, destroy this dark guest within me—the hidden corruption that turns my own heart into a place of misery.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the painful conflict of someone who delights in God’s law yet still finds sin close at hand. This passage gives biblical language for the prayer’s grief over sin that remains active within the heart.

Paul says those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. The prayer draws on this decisive reality while still acknowledging the ongoing struggle to put sin to death in daily practice.

Believers are told to put to death what is earthly in them and to put off old patterns such as malice and slander. This supports the prayer’s plea for God to destroy the sins that continue to rise up.

sections.heading: Remembering that the cross still meets me here
sections.text: But you have not abandoned me to this struggle without grace. The cross still stands, even in the tightest and darkest places of my soul. When I remember my great sins, my many temptations, and my repeated falls, do not let that memory drive me into despair. Let it bring back the greater memory of your help: how you have held me up, rescued me, forgiven me, and given grace to someone as needy as I am. Let the cross preach your deliverance to me again.
theological_themes: the cross as the believer’s refuge
remembering God’s past deliverance as fuel for faith

scripture_references.connection: John holds together honest confession of sin and the cleansing power of Christ’s blood. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that remembering sin need not end in despair because God’s forgiveness is real.

David’s victory over Goliath was explicitly understood as the Lord’s deliverance, not merely human courage. The prayer’s image of remembering a weapon as a sign of rescue draws on that larger story of God saving his servant.
Because Christ is the sympathetic high priest, believers may come for mercy and grace in time of need. This supports the prayer’s claim that the cross meets the soul in its deepest distress.

sections.heading: Asking for more grace to subdue sin
sections.text: There is no treasure I need more than the steady experience of your grace. Only your grace can humble my pride, weaken the sins that keep rising, and teach my heart to live differently. Father, give me more of that grace—not so I can excuse my sin, but so sin loses its power over me and Christ becomes more precious than the approval, anger, and selfish desires I keep chasing.
theological_themes: grace as the power for holiness
Christ becoming more desirable than sin

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that grace not only saves but also trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live for God. This directly supports the prayer’s request for grace that subdues sin rather than merely comforts the sinner.
Paul connects freedom from sin’s dominion with being under grace. This grounds the prayer’s hope that more grace means sin’s power is weakened, not indulged.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses violent self-amputation imagery as a plea for God’s severe mercy against sin. I rendered it as willingness for God to restrain, humble, or remove what feeds sin, while preserving the radical seriousness of the original and its connection to Jesus’ teaching about dealing decisively with sin.

The original’s language about sins being “crucified, forgiven” yet rising again reflects a Protestant already-and-not-yet understanding of sanctification: sin’s reign has been decisively broken in Christ, but remaining sin must still be fought. This can be misunderstood if stated too absolutely, so the adaptation clarifies that sin is judged and forgiven in Christ while its habits still stir in the believer.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “created glory, honour, wisdom, and esteem of others” as the desire to be admired, respected, thought wise, and noticed by people, especially as a hidden motive beneath outwardly good actions.

I retained the concrete image of the “dark guest within” as a way of naming indwelling sin, but avoided making it sound like a separate being or demon possessing the believer. The prayer treats it as hidden corruption within the heart, consistent with the original’s focus on indwelling sin.
I understood the reference to David’s sight of Goliath’s sword as a memory of God’s past deliverance strengthening faith in present need, rather than as a general symbol of power or violence.
